Cube Counting Ambiguity

GeometryCounting
Game: This picture shows little cubes that can be counted in two different ways.
How to play: Drag the purple dot or use the sliders to turn the view. Look carefully and decide whether you see seven cubes or eight.

Look for the math

The same lines can draw two different piles of cubes. Nothing in the picture has to change for your answer to change.

One drawing, two readings

The picture is a flat Necker cube in disguise. Its slanted lines say “this edge goes back”, but they do not say how far back. Without that clue, your mind chooses a reading, and a moment later it may choose the other one. The applet's page puts it plainly: you may see either seven cubes or eight, and staring at the picture can flip which count you believe.

Why the count can change by one

In an oblique projection one rhombus can be a side of two different cubes: in this drawing rhombus 16 is the left face under one diamond and the right face above another. If you group it with the first diamond you get one cube; group it with the second and the cubes shift, so the total changes by one. The logic test finds this shared face by matching every side rhombus against every diamond.

What the three sliders really do

The slant runs from 15° to 60°; its cosine sets the width of a cube face and its sine sets the height. The size runs from 2 to 10 and scales everything by round(height / 1.4 / (N + 5)). The fading runs from −127 to 127 and sets an opacity of min(255, 255 ± 2T). The test checked all 46 × 9 × 255 combinations at two canvas sizes: every one paints the same 33 rhombi in the same order, so the sliders change the view, never the answer.

Try the fading slider: the hidden corner appears, and the count you first chose stops feeling so certain.
